**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: three hours.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will be penalised.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised composition will be severely sanctioned.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **e)** Say what you consider to be the devastating effects of war on a people and how it can be resolved.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: war undoes generations of work.
2. Effects on people: deaths, refugees, broken families, child soldiers.
3. Effects on the economy, education, the mind and the environment.
4. Resolution: dialogue and mediation, root causes, inclusive government.
5. After the war: disarmament, rebuilding, justice and reconciliation; conclusion.

**Model composition (527 words)**

War is the most destructive of all human enterprises. In a few weeks it can undo what a people have built in generations, and its wounds often remain open long after the last gun has fallen silent. Because it leaves nothing untouched, we must understand its effects clearly and, above all, learn how it can be resolved.

The first and most obvious effect is the loss of human life. Soldiers die on the battlefield, but a large share of the victims of modern wars are civilians, among them women, children and the elderly, who are killed in attacks or die from the hunger and disease that spread when hospitals are destroyed. Those who survive are frequently forced to flee. Millions of refugees and internally displaced people live in camps, without homes, schools or regular food, and they depend on the charity of strangers. Families are broken, children become orphans, and some boys are recruited as child soldiers who lose their childhood before they have lived it.

War also ruins the economy. Farms are abandoned, so harvests fail and famine follows. Roads, bridges, factories and power stations are bombed or looted, trade stops, and prices rise beyond the reach of ordinary people. Investors withdraw, businesses close and unemployment grows. A country which spends its wealth on weapons has nothing left for education or health, so that a whole generation grows up without schooling and without skills. Moreover, the psychological damage is enormous: survivors of violence suffer nightmares, depression and distrust, and entire communities are divided by hatred and the desire for revenge. Even nature is a victim, since forests are burnt and rivers are polluted.

How, then, can war be resolved? The first answer is dialogue. Warring parties must be brought to the negotiating table, with the help of neutral mediators such as the African Union, regional organisations and the United Nations. Ceasefires should be respected, prisoners exchanged and humanitarian aid allowed to reach those in need. Yet peace agreements fail when they ignore the root causes of the conflict. Leaders must therefore address the injustices that provoke violence, including exclusion, poverty, corruption, abuse of power and the unfair sharing of natural resources. Inclusive government, in which every group feels represented, is the surest guarantee against new violence.

After the fighting, rebuilding begins. Former fighters need to be disarmed and offered training and jobs, so that they do not return to the bush. Schools and hospitals must be reopened, and refugees helped to return home. Justice is also necessary, for those who have committed atrocities must answer for them, while truth and reconciliation commissions can help victims and offenders to live side by side. Religious leaders, women's groups, teachers and the media can all contribute by preaching tolerance rather than hatred.

In conclusion, war brings death, poverty, trauma and division, and no victory can justify such a price. The wisest course is to prevent it by respecting rights, sharing power fairly and settling disputes through talk. Where it has already begun, honest dialogue, justice and patient reconstruction are the only roads back to peace. A people at peace may argue, but a people at war can only mourn.

**Marking grid (20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Dealing only with the effects of war and forgetting the second part of the topic, how it can be resolved.
2. Naming real conflicts with invented facts; keep to general, verifiable statements.
